problem: Code 0010 is the right-hand bit (value 2, x > xmax), not the below bit. The answer says the second end point is cut against y = ymin, which is bit 2 (value 4, code 0100). With codes 0001 and 0010 both ends lie beyond vertical boundaries, so the y-clipping story in the answer is wrong.
fix: AND = 0000, so no rejection; the codes differ, so it is not accepted either. Code 0001 marks an end left of the window and code 0010 marks an end right of it, so one end is cut against x = xmin and the other against x = xmax. Then the codes are recomputed: if the two new y-values still put both ends beyond the same horizontal boundary the line is rejected, otherwise it is clipped again against y = ymin or y = ymax.

problem: The bit list is garbled: 'Bit 2, value 4: y  xmax, right.' The comparison signs and the whole definition of bit 1 (value 2, right) are missing, and bit 2 is described as if it were the right bit. A student cannot recover the correct four-bit assignment from this line.
fix: Bit 3, value 8: y > ymax (above). Bit 2, value 4: y < ymin (below). Bit 1, value 2: x > xmax (right). Bit 0, value 1: x < xmin (left). Inside or on the boundary: 0000.

where: Worked example 1 step 9, Exam traps bullet 3, Quiz Q1 answer
problem: The same missing comparison signs appear in three more places: 'The p  0 rows give u2 = ...', 'p  0 tightens u2 with min', and 'Below y  xmax: 2' in the Q1 answer. The values are right but the printed text is unreadable.
fix: Step 9: 'The p > 0 rows give u2 = min(1, 5/6, 5/6) = 5/6.' Trap: 'p < 0 tightens u1 with max; p > 0 tightens u2 with min; swapped, an invisible line gets drawn.' Q1 answer: 'Above y > ymax: 8. Below y < ymin: 4. Right x > xmax: 2. Left x < xmin: 1. Inside: 0000.'

problem: Saying a crossing segment 'becomes a shorter segment whose new end points sit on the boundary' suggests both new end points move. Often only one end moves; the other is an original point already inside the window.
fix: At least one new end point sits on a boundary; the other may be an original point that was already inside.

problem: Cyrus–Beck is not simply 'the three-dimensional version'. It is the general parametric clipping algorithm for any convex clip region, in 2D or 3D; Liang–Barsky is its axis-aligned rectangle case.
fix: Cyrus–Beck generalises the same parametric idea to any convex clip region, so clipping against the six planes of a three-dimensional view volume is one use of it.
